key_terms.meaning: Send an electromagnetic wave, time the echo, and use the echo delay and antenna angle to get range and direction.
R = c Δt / 2, where R is range in m, c is speed of light (3×10⁸ m/s), and Δt is round-trip echo delay in s.
Transmitter → duplexer → antenna → target → antenna → receiver → signal processor → display, with a timer controlling pulse transmission.
Named bands such as L, S, C, X and Ku; higher bands give finer resolution and smaller antennas but suffer more rain loss.
P_r = P_t G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ R⁴), where P_r is echo power, P_t transmit power, G antenna gain, λ wavelength, σ target RCS and R range.
Received echo power falls as 1/R⁴, so doubling range needs 16 times the transmit power or antenna gain.
R_max = [P_t G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ S_min)]^(1/4), where S_min is the minimum detectable echo power.
S_min is the weakest echo the receiver can distinguish from noise at a chosen detection and false-alarm probability.
σ is the equivalent echoing area of a target in m² (or dBsm); it depends on shape, aspect angle, material and wavelength.
f_p = 1/T_p is the number of pulses per second, where T_p is the pulse repetition interval in s.
R_u = c/(2 f_p), the largest range whose echo returns before the next pulse is transmitted.
τ is pulse duration in s; range resolution ΔR = cτ/2, and the same-antenna blind range is also about cτ/2.
f_d = 2 v_r / λ for a monostatic radar, where v_r is radial velocity in m/s and λ is wavelength in m; closing targets give positive f_d.
CW radar transmits continuously and measures only Doppler; FMCW adds a linear sweep and uses beat frequency f_b = 2 R Δf/(c T_m), where Δf is sweep bandwidth and T_m is sweep time.
Moving target indication filters out echoes with near-zero Doppler, such as ground clutter, by comparing successive pulses.
v_b = n λ f_p /2, n = 1,2,...; at these radial speeds the Doppler shift equals a multiple of the PRF and MTI cancels the target.
A single pulse is received in sum (Σ) and difference (Δ) beams; the angle error is proportional to Δ/Σ.
The filter with impulse response matched to the known pulse; it maximizes peak signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant in white noise.
Constant false alarm rate detector sets its threshold from a local noise estimate so the false-alarm probability stays fixed as noise changes.
A circulator or transmit-receive tube that connects one antenna to the transmitter and receiver while protecting the receiver from high transmit power.

takeaways: A radar makes one basic measurement—echo delay gives range, antenna pointing angle gives direction—and every other block supports that measurement.
Echo power falls as the fourth power of range, so long range is bought with high transmit power, high antenna gain, low receiver noise or a larger target cross section.
Radar cross section is an equivalent echoing area set by shape, aspect and wavelength, not simply by the physical area of the target.
PRF fixes the largest unambiguous range, while pulse width fixes range resolution and the short-range blind zone.
Doppler shift gives radial velocity; CW radar measures only velocity, while FMCW radar adds range from the beat frequency of a frequency sweep.
MTI and pulse Doppler radar reject stationary clutter, but their blind speeds follow from wavelength and PRF.
Tracking radar forms an angle error from two or more squinted beams, and monopulse gets that error from a single pulse using sum and difference channels.
The matched filter is the best receiver for a known pulse in white noise, and CFAR keeps the false-alarm rate steady as noise changes.
Real radar hardware adds a high-gain antenna, modulator and transmitter, low-noise receiver, duplexer, display and propagation effects to the basic block diagram.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine the block diagram with the range equation, then connect PRF, Doppler, MTI and detection thresholds to practical range and resolution.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a pulse radar and state the function of each block.
outline: Transmitter and modulator generate the high-power pulse
Duplexer shares the antenna and protects the receiver
Antenna radiates and receives the echo
Receiver amplifies and detects the weak echo
Signal processor and display extract range and angle
Timer sets pulse timing and echo delay gives range

bank.q: Explain radar frequency bands and the trade-offs in choosing a radar frequency.
outline: Common bands: L, S, C, X, Ku
Lower frequency: longer range, less rain loss, larger antenna
Higher frequency: finer resolution, smaller antenna, more atmospheric loss
Applications guide the choice
Band names are approximate, not strict borders

bank.q: Derive the radar range equation and define every term in it.
outline: Power density at range R from a directive antenna
Target intercepts power and reradiates with RCS σ
Echo power density back at the radar
Effective aperture of receiving antenna
Final form P_r = P_t G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ R⁴)
Define P_t, G, λ, σ, R and assumptions

bank.q: Define radar cross section and explain why it is not the same as physical area.
outline: Equivalent echoing area in m² or dBsm
Depends on shape and material
Depends strongly on aspect angle
Depends on wavelength relative to target features
Flat plates, corners and engines can give large RCS
Small physical objects can have large or small RCS

bank.q: A radar has PRF 1 kHz. Find its unambiguous range and the largest PRF for an unambiguous range of 150 km.
outline: Use R_u = c/(2 f_p)
Substitute f_p = 1000 Hz to get 150 km
Largest PRF is 1 kHz
State that higher PRF reduces unambiguous range

bank.q: A pulse radar has pulse width 1 μs. Find its range resolution and the blind range for a common transmit/receive antenna.
outline: Range resolution ΔR = cτ/2
Substitute τ = 1×10⁻⁶ s
ΔR = 150 m
Blind range is about cτ/2 = 150 m
Duty cycle also depends on PRF

bank.q: A 10 GHz Doppler radar measures a 100 Hz shift from a car. Find the radial speed of the car.
outline: Use f_d = 2 v_r / λ
v_r = f_d λ / 2
State direction from the sign of the Doppler shift

bank.q: An FMCW radar sweeps 100 MHz in 1 ms and measures a 10 kHz beat frequency. Find the target range.
outline: Use f_b = 2 R Δf/(c T_m)
Rearrange R = f_b c T_m/(2Δf)
Substitute f_b = 10 kHz, Δf = 100 MHz, T_m = 1 ms
R = 15 m
Mention that sweep linearity affects accuracy

bank.q: An MTI radar works at λ = 0.03 m with PRF = 2 kHz. Find its first blind speed.
outline: Use v_b = n λ f_p /2 with n = 1
Substitute λ = 0.03 m and f_p = 2000 Hz
v_b = 30 m/s
Higher blind speeds occur at n = 2, 3, ...
Staggered PRF can avoid a single blind speed

bank.q: Compare CW, FMCW and pulse radar for measuring range and radial velocity.
outline: CW: Doppler velocity only, no range
FMCW: range from beat frequency and velocity from Doppler
Pulse: range from echo delay and velocity from pulse-to-pulse phase
Trade-offs in complexity, ambiguity and average power
Choose by application: speed trap, altimeter, surveillance

bank.q: Explain how PRF and pulse width together limit radar range measurements, and discuss ambiguity and resolution trade-offs.
outline: Unambiguous range R_u = c/(2 f_p)
Short-range blind zone and resolution ΔR = cτ/2
High PRF gives short unambiguous range but good Doppler
Long pulse gives more energy but poor resolution
Pulse compression separates energy and resolution
Staggered PRF helps ambiguity and blind speeds

bank.q: Explain the delay-line canceller in MTI radar and describe blind speeds; how does staggered PRF help?
outline: Two-pulse canceller subtracts previous echo from current echo
Stationary clutter has zero Doppler and cancels
Frequency response has nulls at multiples of PRF
Blind speeds v_b = n λ f_p /2
Staggered PRF moves nulls pulse to pulse
Trade-offs in clutter attenuation and Doppler coverage

bank.q: Compare sequential lobing, conical scan and monopulse tracking, and explain why monopulse is preferred against fluctuating targets.
outline: Squinted beams create an angle error signal
Sequential lobing switches beams pulse to pulse
Conical scan rotates one squinted beam
Both need several pulses and suffer from amplitude fluctuations
Monopulse uses sum and difference channels in one pulse
Monopulse gives higher accuracy and update rate at greater complexity

bank.q: Design outline for a long-range small-aircraft radar: discuss range equation, RCS, PRF, antenna, transmitter, receiver, CFAR and duplexer trade-offs.
outline: Start from R_max and identify P_t, G, λ, σ and S_min
Small aircraft RCS needs high power, high gain or low noise
Choose PRF for unambiguous range and Doppler coverage
Use pulse width or pulse compression for resolution
Low-noise receiver and matched filter improve S_min
CFAR keeps false alarms steady in changing clutter
Duplexer and high-power transmitter must protect receiver
Propagation and rain loss reduce real range

glossary.def: The horizontal angle of a target measured from a radar reference direction.
The vertical angle of a target above or below the horizontal plane.
The direction along the antenna axis where gain is maximum.
Unwanted radar echoes from ground, sea, rain, birds or other non-target objects.
The time between the starts of two successive transmitted pulses, T_p = 1/f_p.
The fraction of time the transmitter is on, D = τ/T_p = τ f_p.
A time window that selects echoes from a narrow range interval.
Changing the PRF from pulse to pulse so blind speeds and range ambiguities do not stay fixed.
A radial target speed at which the Doppler shift looks like a multiple of the PRF and an MTI filter cancels the target.
An MTI filter that subtracts a previous pulse echo from the current echo to remove stationary clutter.
A radar that preserves a phase reference from pulse to pulse so Doppler can be measured.
A radar that detects the echo envelope without keeping pulse-to-pulse phase information.
In monopulse, the antenna output proportional to the total received signal.
In monopulse, the antenna output proportional to the angle of the target off boresight.
A tracking method that rotates a squinted beam around boresight and uses the echo amplitude modulation for angle error.
A tracking method that switches between squinted beams and compares their echo amplitudes.
The receiver front-end amplifier designed to add very little noise to the weak echo.
A device that lets one antenna serve both transmitter and receiver while protecting the receiver from transmit power.
A ferrite three-port device that routes microwave power in one direction around its ports.
A protective cover over an antenna that is transparent to radar waves.
An antenna whose beam is steered electronically by controlling the phase of many radiating elements.
An adaptive threshold method that keeps the false-alarm probability fixed as the noise level changes.
A filter matched to a known pulse that maximizes peak signal-to-noise ratio in white noise.
The probability that a target echo crosses the detection threshold.
Bending of radar waves in atmospheric layers that can extend range beyond the normal horizon.
A technique that transmits a long coded pulse and compresses it in the receiver to get short-pulse range resolution.
